clinicalPearls: Non-dihydropyridine agents (verapamil, diltiazem) typically cause bradycardia, heart block and hypotension
Dihydropyridine agents mainly cause vasodilatory hypotension, sometimes with a reflex tachycardia, at least early on
Hyperglycaemia is characteristic and reflects blockade of insulin release, helping distinguish it from beta-blocker poisoning
A relatively preserved conscious level despite marked hypotension is a recognised feature
Management includes calcium, high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy, vasopressors and supportive care
Modified-release preparations can cause delayed and prolonged toxicity requiring extended monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Calcium-channel-blocker overdose blocks L-type calcium channels in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle and in pancreatic islet cells. Reduced calcium entry impairs myocardial contractility and conduction and causes vasodilatation, producing hypotension and, with non-dihydropyridines, bradycardia and block. Blockade of calcium-dependent insulin secretion causes hyperglycaemia and shifts myocardial metabolism away from carbohydrate use, which underlies the benefit of high-dose insulin therapy.
additionalInvestigations: Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial electrocardiograms
Blood glucose (often high) and electrolytes including calcium
Identification of the agent and whether it is a modified-release formulation
Blood gas and lactate for perfusion
redFlags: Refractory hypotension or high-grade heart block
Ingestion of a modified-release preparation with potential delayed collapse
Deteriorating conscious level indicating severe shock
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary with the agent and dose; with prompt high-dose insulin therapy and vasoactive support many recover, but massive or modified-release ingestions can cause prolonged refractory shock and death.
pitfalls: Confusing it with beta-blocker poisoning (glucose typically high versus low)
Failing to anticipate delayed toxicity from modified-release formulations
Discharging too early after a modified-release ingestion
management: Resuscitate with airway, breathing and circulation support and intravenous fluids for hypotension.
Consider gastrointestinal decontamination with activated charcoal when presentation is early, and whole-bowel irrigation for modified-release preparations.
Give intravenous calcium salts to counter channel blockade, repeating as required.
Start high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy with glucose supplementation as a key inotropic treatment, monitoring glucose and potassium.
Add vasopressors and inotropes such as noradrenaline for refractory hypotension, with atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.
Escalate to intravenous lipid emulsion, cardiac pacing or mechanical circulatory support including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in refractory shock.
Provide extended cardiac monitoring after modified-release ingestion given delayed and prolonged toxicity.
